passages.title: Email Correspondence: A Noise Complaint and a Licence Review

emails.subject: Review of the Ferryman's Arms licence — representation
emails.body:
Dear Licensing,

I live directly behind the Ferryman's Arms and I am the resident whose complaints triggered this review. I want to correct the impression the review notice gives, because it says the review follows "complaints from a local resident" and does not say what I complained about.

I did not complain about live music. I have lived here eleven years and the music has never been the problem. I complained about the smoking area, which moved in March from the front of the building to the yard directly under my bedroom window, and about the extractor fan that was installed at the same time and runs until two.

The review notice proposes removing live music from the licence. That would not address either of the things I complained about, and it would close the room where a hundred people go on a Friday, which I do not want and did not ask for.

I would like my representation to be recorded accurately: I am asking for a condition on the smoking area location and the fan's operating hours. I am not asking for a condition on live music, and if the committee removes it on the strength of my complaint then it will have acted on something I did not say.

I have written to the licensee separately to tell him the same thing, because he should not learn my position from a hearing.

Sincerely,
Solveig Aubert-Nkemelu

emails.subject: RE: Review of the Ferryman's Arms licence — representation
emails.body:
Dear Ms Aubert-Nkemelu,

You are right and the notice is wrong. Your complaints are logged under a category called "noise — general", which is what our system offers, and the officer preparing the review drew the live music proposal from the category rather than from your correspondence. Your actual complaints are in the file and describe a fan and a smoking area.

The notice is being reissued with the correct grounds. The live music proposal is withdrawn — not because you have asked for it to be, though you have, but because there was never any evidence for it.

I want to be clear about the limits of what I can promise. The committee decides, not me. I can put the smoking area and the fan hours before them as the proposed conditions, and I can ensure your representation is quoted rather than summarised. I cannot tell you what they will decide, and I would not want the reissued notice to read as though the outcome were settled.

Two further points.

Our complaint categories do not distinguish between music, plant noise and patron noise, which is how this happened. I have asked for that to change. Every review this office has produced in two years drew its proposed conditions from the same categories, and I do not know how many others describe something the complainant did not raise.

And thank you for writing to the licensee. He telephoned this morning having received your letter, and the conversation was considerably easier than it would have been at a hearing.

Regards,
Desmond Okonkwo
Licensing Officer

passages.title: Why Small Music Venues Close
passages.content:
Small venues close at a rate that is usually reported as a consequence of changing tastes, and audiences declining to attend. Where the closures have been studied, that explanation is rarely the operative one. Most closed venues were selling tickets when they closed.

Property is the dominant factor. Small venues typically occupy buildings whose value in an alternative use — flats, offices, retail — exceeds their value as a venue, and they hold short leases. A venue can be full every weekend and still be worth more to its owner empty, which means viability as a business and survival as a tenant are different questions. Reporting that treats closure as evidence of failure conflates the two routinely.

The second factor is a specific and well-documented legal problem. Where residential development is built beside an existing venue, incoming residents may complain about noise the venue has made for decades, and the venue can face conditions or closure despite having been there first. Several jurisdictions have adopted an agent-of-change principle, placing responsibility for soundproofing on whichever party arrives second. Where adopted, it measurably reduces this category of closure — and it works by allocating a cost, not by suppressing complaints, which is why it survives contact with both sides.

The economics of the sector are widely misunderstood in one particular way. Bar revenue, not ticket revenue, sustains most small venues; tickets frequently cover the performers and little else. This means a change in drinking habits, a licensing restriction on hours or a rise in duty affects venues more than any change in music-going does, and it explains why venues can report growing audiences and shrinking margins at the same time without either figure being wrong.

There is a pipeline argument that is often made poorly and is nonetheless sound. Performers who fill large arenas were, without meaningful exception, developed in rooms holding a few hundred people, where the economics of learning to perform are absorbed by the small venue rather than by the artist. Losing that layer does not reduce the number of concerts next year; it reduces the number of performers capable of filling them in a decade, which is a delay long enough that the connection is rarely drawn in policy.

The reasonable conclusion is that small venues are less a cultural amenity that markets happen to support than a piece of infrastructure whose costs and benefits fall on different parties at different times.

passages.title: Should Councils Protect Small Venues From Development?

viewpoints.name: Councillor Marguerite Delacroix-Hale
viewpoints.text: We adopted agent-of-change and I would defend it while accepting it is not the whole answer, which supporters sometimes imply it is. It stops a venue being closed by neighbours who arrived afterwards. It does nothing at all about a landlord who simply declines to renew a lease because flats are worth more, and that is the more common cause. I would rather say that than let the policy be credited with solving a problem it does not touch, because when venues keep closing people will conclude the principle failed.

viewpoints.name: Terrence Abiodun, property developer
viewpoints.text: I build residential and I have no objection to agent-of-change, which is a clear rule I can price. What I object to is being asked to price an unclear one. On my last scheme the venue's operating hours were not in its licence, the licence was under review, and nobody could tell me what noise level I was insulating against. I costed for the worst case and the scheme became marginal. Publish the standard and I will build to it. Uncertainty is more expensive than stringency, and the current arrangement supplies plenty of both.

viewpoints.name: Dr Beatriz Okonkwo, cultural policy researcher
viewpoints.text: The evidence that agent-of-change reduces noise-related closures is good. The evidence that venue protection preserves a music scene is much weaker, because closures driven by lease and land value continue regardless, and those are the majority. I support the principle. I would caution advocates against citing scene-level outcomes it has not been shown to deliver, and I would direct the argument at lease security and business rates, where the money actually decides things and where almost nobody is campaigning.

viewpoints.name: Iona MacAllister, venue operator
viewpoints.text: Agent-of-change saved my building and I am still closing. My lease has fourteen months to run, my landlord will not discuss renewal, and there is a planning application on the site. None of the protections everyone cites operate on any of that. What would have helped is something nobody offers: a right of first refusal, or a lease of a length that lets me invest in the room. I have been told for six years that my venue matters culturally. It has never once been treated as though it does contractually.
